title: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
summary: How dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN with a fixed matrix memory, how the delta rule and gating fix it, how it trains in chunks, and what a fixed state still cannot do.
outcomes: Explain why linear attention can run as an RNN with a constant-size state instead of a growing KV cache
Compute the state updates of linear attention, DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet by hand on a toy sequence
Explain why additive memory collides and how the delta rule and the decay gate each fix a different failure
Compare the parallel, recurrent and chunkwise forms, and derive DeltaNet's chunkwise form (WY, UT transform) by hand
Classify RetNet, Mamba2, GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, KDA and RWKV-7 by their transition matrix
Bound what a fixed state can recall and explain why parity needs negative eigenvalues
Describe how a recurrent state is decoded and cached in serving, unlike a paged KV cache
Estimate the memory saved by a hybrid model such as Qwen3-Next that mixes Gated DeltaNet with attention

lessons.title: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN

blocks.md:
Recall from the attention course: each output is a softmax-weighted average of value vectors, with weights from query-key dot products. During generation the model keeps every past key and value (the **KV cache**), so memory per sequence grows linearly with context length and each new token must read all of it.

Linear attention asks: can we summarize the past in a **fixed-size state** instead, like an RNN, without giving up parallel training?

Count the numbers kept per attention head. Let $d$ be the **head dimension**, the length of each query, key and value vector in one head. For $L$ past tokens the KV cache stores a key and a value per token, $2Ld$ numbers, while a $d \times d$ state stores $d^2$. The two are equal when $2Ld = d^2$, that is at $L = d/2$, so beyond a few dozen tokens the fixed state is smaller.

blocks.title: Numbers stored per head: KV cache vs a d x d state

scenes.caption: Softmax attention stores a key and a value (d numbers each) per past token, so storage is 2Ld and keeps growing. A d x d state stays flat.
With d = 128 the two cross at L = 64 tokens. At 262,144 tokens the KV cache holds 67,108,864 numbers per head versus 16,384 for the state.
Larger heads raise the flat line (d^2) and move the break-even point right, but it is still tiny compared with long contexts.

blocks.md: Katharopoulos et al. (2020) write attention with a general similarity function, sim, in place of the softmax:

blocks.caption: Output i is a weighted sum of the values v_j, where each weight is the similarity of query i to key j, divided by the total similarity so the weights add up to 1.

blocks.md: Softmax uses $\text{sim}=\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt{d})$. If instead $\text{sim}(q,k)=\phi(q)^\top\phi(k)$ for some **feature map** $\phi$ (a fixed function that turns each vector into another vector, so that the similarity becomes a plain dot product of features), matrix products can be regrouped: $(\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top)V = \phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)$. In words: instead of first comparing every query with every key and then multiplying by V, first multiply the keys' features by the values, which gives a small matrix whose size does not depend on L, and let each query multiply that. The right side never builds the $L \times L$ matrix. They used $\phi(x)=\text{elu}(x)+1$ to keep similarities positive. ELU, the exponential linear unit, returns x when x is positive and $e^x-1$ otherwise, so it always stays above minus 1 and elu(x) + 1 is always positive, like the exp in softmax.

Two routes followed. The first kept softmax and approximated it. Performer (Choromanski et al. 2021) uses **positive random features**: $\phi(x)$ is a list of $m$ numbers of the form $e^{w_i^\top x}$ (times a scale), with each $w_i$ a random Gaussian vector, built so that $\phi(q)^\top\phi(k)$ equals the exponential kernel *in expectation*, that is on average over the random draw. Any single draw is noisy, and the authors take $m$ on the order of $d\log d$ features to make the error small. In practice it did not beat simpler maps: on WikiText-103 language modeling (about 103 million words of Wikipedia articles), Schlag et al. measured test perplexity 39.6 for a small Performer, 38.3 for the elu + 1 linear Transformer and 34.1 for softmax attention of the same size (lower is better).

The second route went after the denominator. Qin et al. (2022) showed that the gradient of a normalized weight $p_j=s_j/\sum_i s_i$ with respect to a score can be as large as $1/(4s)$, so tiny scores mean huge gradients. Tiny scores are easy to get: with elu + 1 features and entries of q and k near minus 4, every feature is $e^{-4}\approx0.018$, and a 2-dimensional score is about 0.00067.

Two scores of 0.0001 give weights 0.5 and 0.5. Nudge the first score by 0.0001 and its weight jumps to 0.67. With scores of 1 and 1, the same nudge moves it only to 0.500025. Simply deleting the denominator was no cure either: in their ablation, validation perplexity went from 4.98 to 797. What worked was normalizing the *output* instead (an RMSNorm on $Q(K^\top V)$: divide the vector by the root mean square of its entries, then scale by learned weights, a cheaper cousin of LayerNorm), and GLA and Gated DeltaNet likewise normalize each head's output before the output projection.

Later work kept that recipe, dropping the denominator (the sum of similarities that made the weights add up to 1) and normalizing the output instead, and simplified further with $\phi$ = identity, as the DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet papers do in their notation. With a causal mask, the output for token $t$ is then:

blocks.tex: o_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t} v_i\,(k_i^{\top}q_t)=\Big(\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t} v_i k_i^{\top}}_{S_t}\Big)q_t,\qquad S_t=S_{t-1}+v_t k_t^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}
blocks.caption: The state S_t is a running sum of outer products v k transpose. Each step adds one rank-1 matrix and reads the output as S_t times q_t: an RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state.

blocks.md: The step from the left side to the right is one line of algebra: $k_i^\top q_t$ is a single number, so scaling $v_i$ by that number gives the same vector as multiplying the matrix $v_ik_i^\top$ by $q_t$, and then $q_t$ can be pulled out of the sum. Here $d_k$ is the length of keys and queries and $d_v$ the length of values (often both equal the head dimension $d$). The **outer product** $v_tk_t^\top$ is the $d_v \times d_k$ matrix whose entry in row i, column j is entry i of $v_t$ times entry j of $k_t$. Every row is a multiple of $k_t^\top$, which is why it has rank 1.

A toy with $d_k=d_v=2$ and four tokens (numbers chosen by hand):

- keys $k$: (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,0)
- values $v$: (1,2), (3,0), (0,1), (2,2)
- queries $q$: (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (1,1)

Rows of $S$ index value dimensions, columns index key dimensions.

blocks.title: The 2 x 2 state S_t after each token

scenes.caption: Start: S_0 is all zeros. Nothing has been written.
Token 1 adds v k^T = (1,2)(1,0)^T, filling column 1. Output o_1 = S_1 q_1 = (1,2).
Token 2 adds (3,0)(0,1)^T into column 2. With q_2 = (1,1), o_2 sums both columns: (4,2).
Token 3 has key (1,1), so (0,1) is added to both columns. o_3 = S_3 (0,1) = (3,1).
Token 4 adds (2,2) to column 1 again. o_4 = S_4 (1,1) = (6,6). The state never grew: still 4 numbers after 4 tokens.

blocks.prompt: Training wants all outputs at once, not a loop. Compute token 4's output the attention way: weights $k_i^\top q_4$ for i = 1..4, then the weighted sum of values. Do you get (6,6)?
blocks.reveal: Weights are $k_i^\top(1,1)$ = 1, 1, 2, 1. Weighted sum: 1(1,2) + 1(3,0) + 2(0,1) + 1(2,2) = **(6,6)**, the same as $S_4q_4$. Stacking all queries, keys and values as rows of Q, K and V gives the **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$, where M is the causal mask (a lower-triangular matrix of ones that zeroes every future position) and $\odot$ multiplies entry by entry. The parallel form and the recurrent form compute identical numbers; only the order of operations differs.

blocks.title: Parallel form: masked QK^T, compared with softmax

scenes.caption: Linear attention weights: QK^T with the causal mask M zeroing the future. Multiplying by V gives rows (1,2), (4,2), (3,1), (6,6), matching the recurrence.
Row 4 sums to 5, not 1: without softmax or the denominator, weights are raw dot products. Nothing forces them to be a probability distribution.
For contrast, softmax of the same scores divided by sqrt(2): row 4 becomes 0.20, 0.20, 0.40, 0.20. Softmax sharpens and normalizes; no finite d x d state can reproduce it exactly.

blocks.md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

Why can no finite state copy softmax exactly? A similarity that equals a dot product of feature vectors is called a **kernel**. Softmax's similarity is the exponential kernel, and the exponential can be expanded as a power series:

blocks.caption: e to the q transpose k equals the sum over every n of q transpose k to the power n, divided by n factorial.

blocks.md: Each power $(q^\top k)^n$ is itself a dot product, between vectors that list every product of n coordinates of q and of k. Matching every term of the series needs features for every n, infinitely many, so any finite feature map, and any finite state, computes a different function.

Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

blocks.question: A linear-attention layer with $d_k=d_v=128$ per head has generated 10,000 tokens. What does it need to keep per head to generate token 10,001?
options: All 10,000 keys and values, like a KV cache
The 128 x 128 state matrix S
Only the last 128 keys
The full 10,000 x 10,000 attention matrix
blocks.explain: Everything the layer knows about the past is folded into $S_t$, a 128 x 128 matrix (16,384 numbers) regardless of how many tokens came before. That is the RNN view of linear attention.

blocks.question: Why does regrouping $(QK^\top)V$ as $Q(K^\top V)$ fail for softmax attention?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative
The softmax is applied to each row of $QK^\top$ before multiplying by V, so the product cannot be regrouped
Softmax attention uses different key and query dimensions
The causal mask makes regrouping impossible for any attention
blocks.explain: Associativity only holds for plain products. Softmax applies a nonlinear exp and normalization to every entry of $QK^\top$ first. Causal masking alone is fine: the running sum $S_t$ handles it.

lessons.title: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up

blocks.md: Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber (2021) showed linear attention is a **fast weight programmer**: $S$ is a weight matrix that the network rewrites at every token by adding outer products $v_tk_t^\top$, and reading $Sq$ is a lookup. The name contrasts two kinds of weights: ordinary *slow* weights are learned by gradient descent during training and then frozen, while *fast* weights are rewritten by the network itself at every token as it reads. Think of $S$ as an associative memory: store value $v$ under key $k$, retrieve by presenting a key.

blocks.caption: Reading with key k_j returns v_j exactly if k_j has unit length and is orthogonal to every other stored key. Any overlap k_i^T k_j leaks v_i into the answer.

blocks.md:
Toy memory with $d_k=2$ and scalar values ($d_v=1$, so $S$ is a 1 x 2 row). Keys have unit length:

- $k_A=(1,0)$, $k_B=(0,1)$, $k_C=(0.6,0.8)$

The sequence writes A=4, then B=2, then **rewrites** A=1 (the fact changed), then writes C=3. A perfect memory would finally return 1, 2, 3.

blocks.prompt: After the rewrite A=1, the state is $S=4k_A^\top+2k_B^\top+1k_A^\top$. What does reading with $k_A$ return?
blocks.reveal: **5**, not 1. Linear attention can only add: the old value 4 and the new value 1 are summed. There is no instruction for "replace what is stored under this key".

blocks.title: Linear attention memory: reads after each write

scenes.caption: Write A=4: S = (4,0). k_A reads 4. k_C = (0.6,0.8) already reads 2.4 because it overlaps k_A by 0.6.
Write B=2: S = (4,2). k_A and k_B are orthogonal, so both read back exactly: 4 and 2.
Rewrite A=1: S = (5,2). k_A now reads 5, the sum of old and new. Additive memory cannot overwrite.
Write C=3: S = (6.8,4.4). Every read is now wrong (6.8, 4.4, 7.6 instead of 1, 2, 3): the third key cannot be orthogonal to the first two in 2 dimensions.

blocks.md:
Two separate failures showed up:

1. **No overwrite.** Rewriting a key accumulates values instead of replacing them.
2. **Collisions.** At most $d_k$ keys can be mutually orthogonal. Once a head has seen more distinct keys than its key dimension, stored values become superimposed. Schlag et al. call this the memory capacity limitation, and the Gated DeltaNet paper notes that collisions become inevitable once the sequence is longer than the dimension.

This is why early linear Transformers trailed softmax attention on language modeling and especially on **in-context recall** (find a fact stated earlier in the prompt). Softmax attention keeps every key separately and can pick one out sharply; a fixed $d_k \times d_v$ state must compress.

The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.
Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

blocks.question: A head has $d_k=64$. A prompt states 500 different key facts, each with its own key direction. What happens to recall under plain linear attention?
options: Nothing, because 500 tokens is short
Keys cannot all be orthogonal in 64 dimensions, so reads mix many stored values
Only the last 64 facts are kept and older ones are cleanly deleted
The model switches to softmax attention automatically
blocks.explain: At most 64 directions can be mutually orthogonal. With 500 associations the overlaps $k_i^\top k_j$ are nonzero and every read returns a weighted mixture. Nothing is cleanly deleted either: additive memory never forgets.

blocks.question: In the toy, why did $k_A$ and $k_B$ read back perfectly after the first two writes?
options: Because they were written first
Because the values 4 and 2 are small
Because the keys are unit length and orthogonal, so $k_A^\top k_B = 0$ and nothing leaks
Because S was reset between writes
blocks.explain: Reading $Sk_A = 4(k_A^\top k_A) + 2(k_B^\top k_A) = 4\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 = 4$. Orthonormal keys make the memory exact; overlap is what causes interference.

lessons.title: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add

blocks.md: DeltaNet (Schlag et al. 2021, scaled up by Yang et al. 2024) replaces the additive write with the **delta rule**, also called the Widrow-Hoff or least mean squares rule, which Bernard Widrow and Ted Hoff published in 1960 to train adaptive linear units. Before writing, it reads what memory currently returns for the key, $v^{\text{old}}_t=S_{t-1}k_t$. It then blends in the new value with a **writing strength** $\beta_t\in(0,1)$, computed per token as $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$. Here $x_t$ is the token's input vector, $W_\beta$ is a learned projection, and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid $1/(1+e^{-z})$, which squashes any number into (0, 1). Then it swaps the blend in:

blocks.caption: Subtract the old value's outer product with k_t, then add the blend v_new = beta v_t plus (1 minus beta) v_old. Collecting terms gives S at t minus 1 times (I minus beta k_t k_t transpose), plus beta v_t k_t transpose. Beta = 1 fully replaces the old value; beta = 0 leaves memory unchanged.

blocks.md: The same update is one step of **online gradient descent** (gradient descent that updates after every single example, here after every token) on a regression loss: make the memory map $k_t$ to $v_t$.

blocks.caption: The loss is half the squared error between what memory returns for k_t and the target v_t. Its gradient with respect to S is the error times k_t transpose, and one step of size beta_t down that gradient is exactly the delta rule.

blocks.md: Why that gradient: entry (i, j) of S changes only entry i of $Sk_t$, with slope equal to entry j of $k_t$. So the derivative of the loss for that entry is error i times entry j of $k_t$, which is the outer product of the error with $k_t$. The one half is there to cancel the 2 that comes from differentiating a square.

The "delta" is the prediction error $v_t-S_{t-1}k_t$. Plain linear attention, by contrast, optimizes the linear loss $-\langle Sk_t,v_t\rangle$ (minus the dot product of the read with $v_t$), which rewards adding $v_t$ no matter what is already stored. Its gradient is $-v_tk_t^\top$, so a step of size 1 adds $v_tk_t^\top$: exactly the additive write of lesson 1.

blocks.title: Same writes, delta rule with beta = 1

scenes.caption: Write A=4: memory was empty so v_old = 0 and S = (4,0), the same as linear attention.
Write B=2: v_old = S k_B = 0, S = (4,2). Still identical to linear attention, because k_B is orthogonal to everything stored.
Rewrite A=1: v_old = S k_A = 4, the error is 1 - 4 = -3, so S = (4,2) - 3(1,0) = (1,2). k_A now reads 1, and k_B is untouched at 2.
Write C=3: v_old = 2.2, error 0.8, S = (1.48,2.64). k_C reads exactly 3. The fix along k_C nudges k_A to 1.48 and k_B to 2.64: three keys still collide in 2 dimensions.

blocks.md: The delta rule makes writes **targeted**: it changes $S$ only along the direction $k_t$ (the matrix $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ leaves every direction orthogonal to $k_t$ alone) and by exactly the amount needed to correct the error. It fixes the no-overwrite failure; it cannot raise capacity above $d_k$.

blocks.prompt: Rerun the same four writes with $\beta=0.5$ instead of 1. After the first write (A=4), what does $k_A$ read?
blocks.reveal: **2**. With $\beta=0.5$ the new value is halfway between the old (0) and the target (4). After all four writes the reads are 1.89, 1.52 and 2.35: each write only moves halfway. The model learns $\beta_t$ per token, so it can choose a strong overwrite for important tokens and a light touch for others.

blocks.md: **Stability.** The transition matrix $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ is a generalized Householder matrix. A Householder matrix $I-2uu^\top$, with $u$ of unit length, reflects every vector through the plane orthogonal to $u$; generalized means the 2 is replaced by $\beta_t$ and the key need not have unit length. Its eigenvalues are 1 (with multiplicity $d-1$) and $1-\beta_t\lVert k_t\rVert^2$. Here is where they come from:

blocks.caption: Multiplying the matrix by k_t returns k_t scaled by 1 minus beta_t times the squared length of k_t, so k_t is an eigenvector with that eigenvalue. Any vector orthogonal to k_t passes through unchanged, and there are d minus 1 independent such directions, each with eigenvalue 1.

blocks.md: If that last eigenvalue leaves $[-1,1]$, repeated writes blow up the state. Schlag et al. normalized keys with the L1 norm (the sum of the absolute values of the entries) for this reason; Yang et al. use L2 normalization instead (divide by the ordinary length, the square root of the sum of squares), so $\lVert k_t\rVert=1$ (every key has length 1) and the eigenvalue $1-\beta_t$ stays in $[0,1]$. With $\beta_t=1$ the matrix becomes a projection that erases one direction and keeps the other $d-1$.

Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

Why was DeltaNet not used at scale before 2024? Its original training algorithm was strictly sequential over the sequence, which uses GPUs poorly. Yang et al. (NeurIPS 2024) found a chunkwise parallel algorithm (lessons 5 and 6), trained a 1.3B-parameter DeltaNet on 100B tokens, and reported better perplexity and zero-shot results than Mamba and GLA baselines. Perplexity, from the attention course, is e raised to the average negative log-likelihood per token on held-out text: roughly how many tokens the model is torn between, so lower is better. Zero-shot results are accuracies on benchmark tasks the model was never trained on and is given no worked examples for. Linear attention's chunk trick (lesson 5: add a whole chunk's outer products to the state with one matmul) does not carry over as is: each delta write depends on the current state through $S_{t-1}k_t$, so a chunk's effect on the state is a product of matrices rather than a sum of outer products.

Mamba is a selective **state-space model**: a recurrent layer, borrowed from control theory, that updates a hidden state as $h_t = A_th_{t-1} + B_tx_t$, where *selective* means $A_t$ and $B_t$ are computed from the current token. GLA (gated linear attention, Yang et al. 2024) is linear attention with a learned decay gate on the state, one gate per key channel; lesson 4 adds the simpler one-number version, and lesson 7 compares the two.

blocks.question: Memory holds $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$ with orthogonal unit keys. A token writes $k_A\to1$ with $\beta=1$ using the delta rule. What does $k_B$ read afterwards?
blocks.explain: The update only changes $S$ along $k_A$: $S(I-k_Ak_A^\top)$ leaves the $k_B$ direction untouched because $k_A^\top k_B=0$. So $k_B$ still reads 2, while $k_A$ now reads exactly 1.

blocks.question: Which statement about DeltaNet's $\beta_t$ is correct?
options: It is a fixed hyperparameter shared by all tokens
It is a per-token learning rate in (0,1) for an online regression step
It decays all of memory uniformly at each step
It must equal the norm of the key
blocks.explain: $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$ is computed from the token, and in the gradient-descent view it is the step size. Uniform decay of all memory is a different mechanism (the gate $\alpha_t$ in the next lesson).

lessons.title: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting

blocks.md: A second family of fixes added a **decay gate**. Mamba2 (a selective state-space model, lesson 3) updates a matrix state per head as $h_t=a_th_{t-1}+B_tx_t^\top$ and outputs $y_t=h_t^\top C_t$. Each token supplies a vector $B_t$ that decides where the input is written, a vector $C_t$ that decides what is read, and its input $x_t$, here a whole vector of channels, so the write $B_tx_t^\top$ is an outer product like $v_tk_t^\top$. Line them up with linear attention: $B_t$ plays the key, $C_t$ the query and $x_t$ the value (Dao and Gu tabulate exactly this correspondence). The general SSM transition $A_t$ is a matrix; Mamba2 restricts it to a single number $a_t$ times the identity, and that restriction is what makes the update read as gated linear attention: $S_t=\alpha_tS_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, with $\alpha_t\in(0,1)$ computed from the token. Every association shrinks by the same factor each step. That clears memory quickly, but it is untargeted: to forget one stale fact, everything fades equally.

After n more tokens, a stored association has been multiplied by $\alpha^n$. Its **half-life** is the n where $\alpha^n = 1/2$. Taking logs, $n = \ln(1/2) / \ln\alpha$, which is close to $0.69/(1-\alpha)$ when $\alpha$ is near 1. Two facts give that shortcut. First, $\ln(1/2)$ is minus $\ln 2$, about minus 0.69. Second, near 1 the curve $\ln x$ hugs its tangent line x minus 1, so $\ln\alpha$ is about $\alpha$ minus 1. Dividing the two negatives gives 0.69 over the gap between 1 and $\alpha$. For $\alpha = 0.99$ that is 0.69 over 0.01, about 69 tokens.

blocks.title: How long a memory survives under a constant gate

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.99: half of an association is gone after about 69 tokens, and 0.37 of it remains after 100.
alpha = 0.9: half-life about 6.6 tokens; after 20 tokens only 0.12 remains. Fine for clearing a finished document, fatal for a fact needed later.
alpha = 0.999: half-life about 693 tokens. Real models compute alpha per token, so they can hold near 1 and drop toward 0 at a boundary (simplified: constant here).

blocks.md: The Gated DeltaNet paper (Yang, Kautz, Hatamizadeh, ICLR 2025) observes the two fixes are complementary: **gating enables rapid erasure, the delta rule enables targeted updates.** The gated delta rule simply multiplies the delta transition by $\alpha_t$:

blocks.caption: Equation 10 of the paper. Shrink the old memory by alpha_t, erase along k_t as the delta rule does, then add beta_t v_t k_t transpose; the output is S_t times q_t. alpha_t near 0 wipes the memory; alpha_t = 1 recovers pure DeltaNet; beta_t still sets how strongly the new pair overwrites.

blocks.md: A context-switch toy. Document 1 writes $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$. Document 2 begins and writes $k_A\to1$; on that token we set $\alpha=0.1$ by hand (a trained model would learn to). Document 2 never mentions B, so ideally $k_A$ reads 1 and $k_B$ reads 0. All rules use $\beta=1$ and the unit keys from before.

blocks.title: After the context switch: four update rules

scenes.caption: End of document 1: every rule holds S = (4,2), so k_A reads 4 and k_B reads 2.
Linear adds: k_A = 5, k_B = 2 stale. Mamba2-style decays then adds: k_A = 0.4 + 1 = 1.4. DeltaNet overwrites A exactly but keeps stale B = 2.
Gated DeltaNet decays to (0.4,0.2), then the delta step corrects A from 0.4 to exactly 1. Result: k_A = 1, k_B = 0.2. Only it gets both right (alpha = 0 would give 0).

blocks.title: The gated delta rule as a loop
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def gated_delta(keys, vals, alphas, betas):
    S = np.zeros(2)        # d_v = 1, d_k = 2
    for k, v, a, b in zip(keys, vals, alphas, betas):
        S = a * S          # gate: decay all memory
        v_old = S @ k      # what memory says for k
        S = S + b * (v - v_old) * k  # delta step
    return S

kA, kB = np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([0., 1.])
S = gated_delta([kA, kB, kA], [4., 2., 1.],
                alphas=[1., 1., 0.1], betas=[1., 1., 1.])
print(S @ kA, S @ kB)

scenes.caption: Token 1 (k_A, v = 4, alpha = 1): nothing to decay, v_old = 0, so the delta step writes 4 along k_A.
Token 2 (k_B, v = 2, alpha = 1): v_old = S @ k_B = 0 (@ is Python's matrix-multiply operator), so 2 is written along k_B.
Token 3 (k_A, v = 1, alpha = 0.1): the gate shrinks S to [0.4, 0.2].
v_old = 0.4. The delta step adds (1 - 0.4) along k_A, giving [1.0, 0.2].
Reads: k_A gives 1.0, k_B gives 0.2. Real kernels do the same per head with S of shape d_v x d_k and vector values.

blocks.md: **Online-learning view.** Table 1 of the paper writes each rule as the exact minimizer of a per-token objective. DeltaNet's objective is:

blocks.caption: Stay close to the old memory (the Frobenius norm squared: square every entry of the difference and add them up), while rewarding a read S_t k_t that points along the correction, beta_t times the error.

blocks.md: Set its gradient with respect to $S_t$ to zero. The first term gives twice the difference between the new and old memory, and the second gives minus 2 times the correction times $k_t^\top$. So the new memory equals the old memory plus $\beta_t$ times the error times $k_t^\top$: the delta rule. Gated DeltaNet replaces $S_{t-1}$ with $\alpha_tS_{t-1}$. In the stochastic gradient descent picture (one gradient step per example), $\beta_t$ is the learning rate and $\alpha_t$ is an adaptive **weight decay** on the fast weights: weight decay multiplies the weights by a number just below 1 at each step, pulling them toward zero.

The paper tests recall with S-NIAH (single needle in a haystack), taken from RULER, a 2024 NVIDIA benchmark built to measure how much of its advertised context length a model can really use: one key-value fact, the needle, is hidden in a long context, the haystack, and the model must return the value when asked for the key. Its three variants hide a pass-key number in repeated filler text, a number in real essays, and a UUID in real essays; the paper labels them S-NIAH-1, 2 and 3. A UUID (universally unique identifier) is a 128-bit random label written as 32 hexadecimal digits in five dash-separated groups, so recalling it means reproducing a long, meaningless string exactly.

blocks.md: Next, the full layer. A **token mixer** is the layer that moves information between positions, the job attention does in a Transformer. A short causal convolution mixes each position with the few positions just before it, using learned weights and never looking ahead. SiLU is the activation $x\cdot\sigma(x)$, x times its sigmoid. The gate is built as $\alpha = e^{g}$ with g equal to minus a learned positive rate (exp of A_log: the rate is stored as its logarithm, so exp always turns it back into a positive number) times softplus of a token-dependent number plus a learned bias (dt_bias, where dt is Mamba's name for its step size, delta t); softplus, $\ln(1+e^x)$, is always positive, so g is negative and $\alpha$ lands in (0, 1). Between mixers sit SwiGLU MLPs (Shazeer 2020; the name means a gated linear unit, GLU, whose gate uses Swish, another name for SiLU): feed-forward layers that project the input up twice, pass one copy through SiLU, multiply the two entry by entry and project back down. The paper stacks them following the macro architecture of Meta's Llama models.

blocks.question: A model reads a long code file, then a new unrelated file starts. Which mechanism lets a Gated DeltaNet head discard the old file's associations within a few tokens?
options: The delta rule with $\beta_t=1$
L2 normalization of keys
A small $\alpha_t$ at the boundary
The short convolution
blocks.explain: The delta rule only edits the direction of the current key, one association per token, so it cannot clear thousands of stale associations quickly. A small $\alpha_t$ scales the whole state toward zero at once.

blocks.question: In S-NIAH-1 (needle in repeated filler) at 8K, Mamba2 scores 30.4 and DeltaNet 98.8. What is the best explanation?

DeltaNet uses softmax attention for long inputs
The filler text collides with the needle in DeltaNet only
blocks.explain: The paper's own reading: decay hurts retention. Repeated filler adds little new information, so DeltaNet's lack of forgetting is harmless here, while uniform decay erodes the needle. Gated DeltaNet (91.8) loses a little because it also decays.

lessons.title: Three ways to compute one layer: parallel, recurrent, chunkwise

blocks.md:
Training processes whole sequences, so we want parallel matmuls. Yang et al. (2024) compare three ways to compute the same layer for sequence length $L$, head dimension $d$, chunk size $C$:

- **Parallel form** $(QK^\top\odot M)V$: $O(L^2d+Ld^2)$ FLOPs, all positions at once.
- **Recurrent form**: $O(Ld^2)$ FLOPs but $L$ sequential steps of small elementwise work that cannot use tensor cores (the units inside a GPU that multiply small dense matrix tiles many times faster than ordinary arithmetic units, so they only help when the work is shaped as matmuls).
- **Chunkwise form**: $O(LCd+Ld^2)$ FLOPs and $L/C$ sequential steps. $C=L$ recovers the parallel form, $C=1$ the recurrent one; in practice $C$ is 64 or 128.

Where the chunkwise count comes from: split the L tokens into $L/C$ chunks of C tokens. Inside a chunk, masked attention over C positions costs about $C^2d$, and $L/C$ chunks cost $LCd$. Passing the state costs a d by C times C by d matmul, $Cd^2$, per chunk, so $Ld^2$ in total.

blocks.md: For plain linear attention the chunkwise form is easy: inside a chunk use the masked parallel form, across chunks pass the state $S_{[t+1]}=S_{[t]}+V_{[t]}^\top K_{[t]}$, where $S_{[t]}$ is the state at the start of chunk t and $V_{[t]}$ and $K_{[t]}$ stack that chunk's C values and keys as rows. The delta rule is harder because each chunk's transition is a product of $C$ Householder-like matrices $\prod(I-\beta_ik_ik_i^\top)$, and materializing a $d\times d$ state per token would cost too much memory traffic.

Lesson 6 derives the fix by hand. In brief, Yang et al. use the classical **WY representation** (Bischof and Van Loan), named after the two stacked matrices of vectors, W and Y, in the form $I - WY^\top$: a product of such matrices equals $I-\sum_i w_ik_i^\top$ for vectors $w_i$ computable from the chunk's keys. A **UT transform** (Joffrain et al. 2006, named after its factors: U holds the vectors and T is a small triangular matrix) gets all $w_i$ (and matching $u_i$ for values) from one small $C\times C$ lower-triangular system, so the work becomes matmuls. The open-source kernels live in FLA (flash-linear-attention), a library of GPU kernels for linear-attention models written in Triton, a Python language for GPU kernels.

blocks.question: You must train a Gated DeltaNet layer on 8K-token sequences on GPUs. Which computation form should the training kernel use?
options: Recurrent form, because it has the fewest FLOPs
Fully parallel form, because it has no sequential steps
Chunkwise form, which keeps FLOPs near linear and turns most work into matmuls with only L/C sequential steps
Any form, they run equally fast
blocks.explain: The recurrent form serializes 8K small updates and cannot use tensor cores well; the parallel form pays $O(L^2d)$ FLOPs. Chunkwise is what FLA and the paper use for training.

lessons.title: Chunkwise DeltaNet derived: WY form and the UT transform by hand

blocks.md:
Lesson 5 left one gap. For linear attention a chunk adds $V^\top K$ to the state, a plain sum. For DeltaNet each token multiplies the state by $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$, so a chunk multiplies it by a product of C such matrices. Two obvious plans fail. Storing every token's $d\times d$ state costs $Ld^2$ numbers of slow GPU memory traffic. A **parallel scan** (a prefix-sum algorithm that combines neighbouring steps in a tree, finishing in about $\log_2 L$ rounds) works in principle, but Songlin Yang's write-up shows each combine multiplies dense $d\times d$ matrices, about $L\log L\,d^3$ work, and still materializes the matrices.

The way out is an old fact from numerical linear algebra: a product of identity-minus-rank-1 matrices stays identity minus a short sum of rank-1 terms, one per factor.

blocks.caption: The WY form of the chunk's transition. Factors are multiplied left to right in token order, matching this course's update S_t = S_{t-1}(I - beta_t k_t k_t^T) + beta_t v_t k_t^T, which multiplies the state on the right.

blocks.md:
Why it holds, by induction. Suppose the first $r-1$ factors multiply to $I-\sum_{i<r}w_ik_i^\top$. Multiply on the right by $I-\beta_rk_rk_r^\top$ and expand: $I-\sum_{i<r}w_ik_i^\top-\beta_rk_rk_r^\top+\beta_r\sum_{i<r}w_i(k_i^\top k_r)k_r^\top$. The last two terms both end in $k_r^\top$, so they merge into one new term $-w_rk_r^\top$ with $w_r$ as above. A $d\times d$ matrix per token becomes one d-vector per token.

The same induction on the state, starting from an empty memory at the chunk's start, gives $S_r=\sum_iu_ik_i^\top$ with **pseudo-values** $u_r=\beta_r\big(v_r-\sum_{i<r}u_i(k_i^\top k_r)\big)$ (Yang et al. 2024, Eq. 7): DeltaNet is linear attention run on corrected values.

A toy chunk, with lesson 3's unit keys $k_A=(1,0)$, $k_B=(0,1)$, $k_C=(0.6,0.8)$, scalar values, and $\beta=1$ on every token (so each factor is a projection). The chunk starts from the state $S_{[t]}=(4,2)$, which is A=4 and B=2 written earlier, and holds three tokens:

1. $k_A\to1$, query $k_B$
2. $k_C\to3$, query $k_A$
3. $k_B\to5$, query $k_C$

The key overlaps are $k_A^\top k_C=0.6$, $k_C^\top k_B=0.8$ and $k_A^\top k_B=0$. Tokens 1 and 2 repeat the last two writes of lesson 3, so the state after them matches its bars: (1, 2), then (1.48, 2.64).

Times I - k_C k_C^T. w_2 = k_C - w_1 (0.6) = (0, 0.8), and I - w_1 k_A^T - w_2 k_C^T = [[0, 0], [-0.48, 0.36]], matching the product.

Yet token 1 still influences token 3 *indirectly*, because it changed $w_2$. That indirect path is exactly what the next step captures in one matrix.

blocks.md: The recursion is still a loop over tokens. Write it for all of them at once: stack the $w_r$ as rows of W and the keys as rows of K. The recursion says $W+\text{tril}(\text{diag}(\beta)KK^\top,-1)\,W=\text{diag}(\beta)K$, where tril(., -1) keeps only the entries strictly below the diagonal (only earlier tokens feed later ones) and diag($\beta$) puts the writing strengths on a diagonal. Solving for W gives the **UT transform**:

blocks.caption: Yang et al. 2024, Eq. 10 and 11. The matrix being inverted is C x C, lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, so it is solved by forward substitution: each row uses only the rows above it.

blocks.title: Building T for the toy chunk (C = 3, beta = 1)

scenes.caption: K K^T: every pair of keys' dot product. 0.6 and 0.8 are the overlaps; k_A and k_B are orthogonal, so the corner is 0.
I + tril(diag(beta) K K^T, -1): keep the strictly lower part (earlier tokens feeding later ones) and put ones on the diagonal.
Its inverse T. The 0.48 in the corner is the indirect path token 1 to token 2 to token 3: (-0.6) times (-0.8). T sums the weight of every path between two tokens.

blocks.md:
Check it: $W=TK$ has rows (1, 0), (0, 0.8), (0, 0.36), the same w's as the recursion, and $U=TV$ with values (1, 3, 5) gives pseudo-values (1, 2.4, 3.08). Yang's blog reads T exactly this way, as a sum over all paths in a small graph whose edge from token i to a later token r has weight $-\beta_rk_i^\top k_r$.

Now the chunk runs like linear attention on corrected values. Each token first subtracts what the incoming state already returns along its $w$: $D=U-WS_{[t]}^\top$. Then:

blocks.caption: Yang et al. 2024, Eq. 8 and 9. The first output term reads the incoming state; the second is causal linear attention inside the chunk on the corrected values D. M includes the diagonal, because o_t reads the state after token t's write.

Intra-chunk part: masked Q K^T rows (0), (1, 0.6) and (0.6, 1, 0.8) times D give 0, -2.52 and 0.888.

blocks.md: The WY form and the UT transform turn C sequential rank-1 updates into one small C x C triangular solve plus matmuls ($KK^\top$, $TK$, $TV$, $WS^\top$, $QK^\top$, $D^\top K$). Only that solve and the hand-off of the state between chunks remain sequential.

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)

def recurrent(q, k, v, beta):            # q, k: [L, dk]  v: [L, dv]  beta: [L]
    S = torch.zeros(v.shape[1], k.shape[1])   # d_v x d_k as in this course
    out = []
    for t in range(len(k)):
        S = S + beta[t] * torch.outer(v[t] - S @ k[t], k[t])   # delta rule
        out.append(S @ q[t])
    return torch.stack(out), S

def chunkwise(q, k, v, beta, C=16):
    S, out = torch.zeros(v.shape[1], k.shape[1]), []
    for s in range(0, len(k), C):
        Q, K, V, b = q[s:s+C], k[s:s+C], v[s:s+C], beta[s:s+C]
        A = torch.tril(b[:, None] * (K @ K.T), -1)    # strictly lower part
        I = torch.eye(len(K))
        T = torch.linalg.solve_triangular(I + A, torch.diag(b), upper=False)
        W, U = T @ K, T @ V                           # UT transform
        D = U - W @ S.T                               # pseudo-values minus old reads
        out.append(Q @ S.T + torch.tril(Q @ K.T) @ D) # inter + intra chunk
        S = S + D.T @ K                               # state for the next chunk
    return torch.cat(out), S

torch.manual_seed(0)
L, dk, dv = 64, 16, 8
q, v = torch.randn(L, dk), torch.randn(L, dv)
k = torch.nn.functional.normalize(torch.randn(L, dk), dim=-1)
beta = torch.rand(L)
o1, S1 = recurrent(q, k, v, beta)
o2, S2 = chunkwise(q, k, v, beta)
print((o1 - o2).abs().max().item(), (S1 - S2).abs().max().item())

blocks.md: **Where Gated DeltaNet's gate goes.** Each transition is now $\alpha_t(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)$. Inside a chunk let $\gamma_r$ be the product of the gates from the chunk's first token through token r. Section 3.3 of the Gated DeltaNet paper changes three things: every $k_i^\top k_r$ in the triangular system and in the masked $QK^\top$ is scaled by $\gamma_r/\gamma_i$, the decay between the two tokens; queries and w's that touch the incoming state are scaled by $\gamma_r$; and the state handed on is decayed by $\gamma_C$, with each key scaled by $\gamma_C/\gamma_r$. FLA stores $g=\ln\alpha$ and takes a cumulative sum, so every ratio is the exponential of a difference.

blocks.code:
def gated_chunkwise(q, k, v, beta, g, C=16):    # g = log(alpha), one per token
    S, out = torch.zeros(v.shape[1], k.shape[1]), []
    for s in range(0, len(k), C):
        Q, K, V, b = q[s:s+C], k[s:s+C], v[s:s+C], beta[s:s+C]
        c = g[s:s+C].cumsum(0)                     # log gamma_r
        G = torch.tril((c[:, None] - c[None, :]).exp())   # gamma_r / gamma_i
        A = torch.tril(b[:, None] * (K @ K.T) * G, -1)
        T = torch.linalg.solve_triangular(torch.eye(len(K)) + A, torch.diag(b), upper=False)
        W, U = T @ (K * c.exp()[:, None]), T @ V
        D = U - W @ S.T
        out.append((Q * c.exp()[:, None]) @ S.T + ((Q @ K.T) * G) @ D)
        S = c[-1].exp() * S + D.T @ (K * (c[-1] - c).exp()[:, None])
    return torch.cat(out), S
blocks.caption: Drop-in gated version of the function above. On random inputs with g in (-0.5, 0) it matches a token-by-token gated loop to 2e-15 and, in a separate run, FLA's naive_chunk_gated_delta_rule to 7.5e-07 (FLA runs in float32).

blocks.question: In the toy, $k_A^\top k_B=0$, yet $T$ has 0.48 in row 3, column 1. Why?
options: Rounding error in the triangular solve
Because beta = 1 makes T symmetric
Because the diagonal of T is always 1

blocks.question: Which step of chunkwise DeltaNet keeps a token-by-token dependency inside a chunk?
options: The forward substitution that solves for T
Computing $QK^\top$ for the chunk
Multiplying $T$ by $V$

blocks.explain: Row r of T depends on rows 1 to r - 1, so forward substitution is inherently ordered, but it is only a C x C system. Everything else is a dense matmul. Across chunks, the state hand-off is the other sequential part.

lessons.title: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA

blocks.md:
Every model so far updates a matrix state the same way: multiply the old state on the right by a **transition matrix** $A_t$ (size $d_k\times d_k$, acting on key directions), then add a write. Recent papers describe new layers mostly by what $A_t$ is.

Tiny example: $S=(4,2)$ holds A=4 in key channel 1 and B=2 in channel 2. The identity keeps (4, 2). A scalar 0.5 gives (2, 1). A diagonal Diag(0, 1) gives (0, 2): it forgets A and keeps B. The Householder-like $I-k_Ak_A^\top$ also gives (0, 2), by erasing the $k_A$ direction.

blocks.md: **The decay branch.** RetNet (Sun et al. 2023) uses $A=\gamma I$ with a fixed $\gamma=1-2^{-5-h}$ for head h, so heads forget at different speeds: 0.969 for the first head (half-life about 22 tokens), 0.984 for the second (about 44). Mamba2 makes the scalar token-dependent, $\alpha_t$ (lesson 4). GLA (Yang et al. 2024) goes further with $A_t=\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)$, a vector of gates in (0, 1), one per key channel, computed from the token through a small low-rank layer; the RWKV-7 paper lists RWKV-6 with the same form. The GLA authors place this between a single scalar gate (the form Mamba2 later adopted) and a full outer-product gate, which gave only marginal gains in their preliminary experiments.

blocks.title: Forget A, keep B: what each transition can do in one step

scenes.caption: Start: S = (4, 2) with A in key channel 1 and B in channel 2. The next token should drop A and keep B.
Scalar gate 0.9 (Mamba2-style): (3.6, 1.8). B survives, but A barely fades.
Scalar gate 0.1: (0.4, 0.2). A is nearly gone, and so is B. A single number cannot treat the channels differently.
Diagonal gate Diag(0.1, 1) (GLA, KDA): (0.4, 2). A fades, B is untouched.
Delta write v = 0 along k_A with beta = 1 (DeltaNet): (0, 2). It works too, but it spends the token's one write. Simplified: here each fact sits in one key channel.

blocks.md:
**The delta branch.** DeltaNet's $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ is identity plus a rank-1 correction; Gated DeltaNet scales it by $\alpha_t$. Kimi Delta Attention (KDA, Kimi Team 2025) replaces that per-head scalar with a per-channel $\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)$: $A_t=\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)$ in this course's orientation (the paper stores the transposed state, so it writes the factors in the other order). RWKV-7 (Peng et al. 2025) uses $\text{Diag}(w_t)-\hat\kappa_t(a_t\odot\hat\kappa_t)^\top$ (written with this course's column vectors; the paper uses row vectors, so it puts the transpose on the first factor): a per-channel decay $w_t$ minus a rank-1 erase along a normalized key $\hat\kappa_t$, with its own per-channel in-context learning rate $a_t$. The paper calls this a generalized delta rule.

Both are **diagonal plus low rank (DPLR)** matrices. KDA ties both low-rank vectors to the key, and the Kimi team reports that this roughly doubles kernel speed over a general DPLR kernel.

**The objective view.** Table 1 of the Gated DeltaNet paper writes each update as the exact minimizer of a per-token objective: stay close to the old state, plus a term about the new pair. Linear attention and Mamba2 reward the plain dot product $\langle Sk_t,v_t\rangle$ (Mamba2 measures closeness to the decayed state $\alpha_tS_{t-1}$). DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet reward the correction toward $v_t$, as in lesson 4. Longhorn (Liu et al. 2024) minimizes $\lVert S-S_{t-1}\rVert_F^2+\beta_t\lVert Sk_t-v_t\rVert^2$ exactly instead of taking one gradient step, which gives a delta update with step $\beta_t/(1+\beta_tk_t^\top k_t)$ (the paper uses a per-channel $\beta_t$ and, for speed, a diagonal approximation of that transition).

Titans (Behrouz et al. 2024) pushes this **learning at test time** view furthest: the memory is a small MLP trained on $\lVert M(k_t)-v_t\rVert^2$ while the context streams by, with momentum and a weight-decay gate. With a linear memory and no momentum, it is a decay plus one delta step, nearly the gated delta rule.

**What each costs in a chunkwise kernel.** A scalar decay (RetNet, Mamba2) only rescales each entry of the masked $QK^\top$ by one ratio $\gamma_r/\gamma_i$, so the chunk stays pure matmuls; in the Gated DeltaNet paper's measurements Mamba2 trains slightly faster than DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. A per-channel decay puts a different ratio in every channel of every pair. Cumulative products of gates in (0, 1) underflow over a chunk, so GLA computes them in log space, $\exp(\log b_{rk}-\log b_{ik})$ per channel k, which cannot run as a half-precision tensor-core matmul; GLA recovers speed with a second, smaller level of chunks and keeps only the innermost part in full precision. Delta rules add lesson 6's $C\times C$ triangular solve. KDA has both costs, which is why its constrained DPLR form matters.

Summary, one model per line (transition; write rule; chunkwise cost):

- **Linear attention**: $I$; additive; plain matmuls.
- **RetNet**: fixed $\gamma I$; additive; matmuls with a fixed decay mask.
- **Mamba2**: $\alpha_tI$; additive; matmuls with a data-dependent decay mask.
- **GLA, RWKV-6**: $\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)$; additive; log-space per-channel decay, two-level chunks.
- **DeltaNet**: $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$; delta; triangular solve plus matmuls.
- **Gated DeltaNet**: $\alpha_t(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)$; delta; as DeltaNet plus scalar decay ratios.
- **KDA**: $\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)(I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top)$; delta; triangular solve plus per-channel decay.
- **RWKV-7**: $\text{Diag}(w_t)$ minus rank 1; generalized delta; general DPLR kernel.

To place a new linear-attention layer, ask two questions. What is $A_t$: identity, scalar, diagonal, identity minus rank 1, or diagonal plus low rank? And what does the write minimize: a dot-product reward (additive) or a regression error (delta)? Richer $A_t$ means finer forgetting and a costlier kernel.

blocks.question: A head keeps a variable's value in key channel 3 and the current topic in key channel 7. The next token should drop the variable but keep the topic, and its own write is needed for something else. Which transition can do this?
options: Mamba2's scalar $\alpha_tI$
RetNet's fixed $\gamma I$
A per-channel $\text{Diag}(\alpha_t)$, as in GLA or KDA
DeltaNet's $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ alone
blocks.explain: Only a diagonal gate can scale channel 3 toward 0 while leaving channel 7 near 1. Scalar gates shrink both equally. The delta rule could erase channel 3, but only by spending this token's single write on it.

blocks.question: Why does GLA's chunkwise kernel need log-space arithmetic and a second level of chunks, while Mamba2's does not?
options: GLA uses softmax inside each chunk
GLA's per-channel gate products differ in every channel and underflow over a chunk, so they cannot be folded into one half-precision matmul
Mamba2 has no chunkwise form and runs only as a recurrence
GLA's state is a vector, not a matrix
blocks.explain: With a scalar gate, one ratio per token pair rescales the whole $QK^\top$ entry. With a gate per channel, each channel needs its own ratio of cumulative products, which GLA computes as exponentials of log differences in full precision, then recovers speed with sub-chunks.

lessons.title: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking

blocks.md:
A fixed state has two separate limits, and they need different fixes.

- **Recall**: a prompt says "Ana's extension is 4417" and, 3,000 tokens later, asks for it. The answer must have been stored somewhere. This is about *how much* the state can hold.
- **State tracking**: a prompt lists 200 swap instructions and asks whether an odd number of them touched the first item. Nothing needs to be stored except one bit, but the state must *flip* correctly at every step. This is about *which updates* the transition can express.

**Recall, measured.** Zoology (Arora et al. 2023) trained 17 language models from 70M to 1.4B parameters and found attention-free gated-convolution models trailing attention by up to 2.1 perplexity on the Pile (a large open English text collection assembled by EleutherAI). 82% of that gap came from **associative recall** tokens, the ones predictable by looking up an earlier pair in the context, though they are only 6.4% of tokens; a 70M attention model beat a 1.4B Hyena model (a gated-convolution architecture, 20 times larger) on them. They formalized the task as **MQAR** (multi-query associative recall): many key-value pairs, then many queries.

Based (Arora et al. 2024) varied the state size of many architectures and found MQAR accuracy rising with state size in every architecture class, a recall-memory trade-off that Based itself tries to push outward. They prove any recurrent model needs a state that grows at least linearly with the input length to solve MQAR.

**Copying, proved.** Jelassi et al. (2024) call every fixed-state model a generalized state space model (GSSM) and give a counting argument: if the state has fewer bits than the string to be copied, it cannot tell all strings apart, so it must fail on many of them. Precisely, for strings of L symbols drawn uniformly from an alphabet of D symbols:

blocks.caption: Jelassi et al. 2024, Corollary 2.8. In contrast, they construct a two-layer Transformer that copies strings whose length is exponential in its number of heads.

blocks.md:
Worked numbers for one Gated DeltaNet head with a $128\times128$ state stored in 16-bit numbers (lesson 9 assumes 32-bit, which would double every count below): 16,384 numbers times 16 bits is 262,144 bits, 32 KiB.

- **Random 32-bit values** (say, keys the model will later ask about, each with a random 32-bit answer): no encoding fits more than 262,144 / 32 = 8,192 of them.
- **Copying text**: Qwen3-Next's vocabulary has 151,936 tokens, $\log_2$ of which is 17.2 bits, so one head cannot copy more than about 15,229 tokens with better than even odds.
- **A 4K-token prompt** with one 32-bit fact per token needs 131,072 bits, which still fits the count.

So for one head at 4K tokens the information bound is not what bites. The linear read-out is: lesson 2 showed about $d_k=128$ clean associations per head, 64 times fewer than 8,192.

blocks.title: What one 128 x 128 head (16-bit) could hold, by bound

scenes.caption: Counting bound: 262,144 bits can hold at most 8,192 random 32-bit values, under any encoding.
Copying Qwen3-Next tokens at 17.2 bits each: at most about 15,229 tokens before failure becomes more likely than success.
A 4K prompt of key-value pairs is under both bounds, so counting alone does not forbid recalling it.
But a linear read-out has only about d_k = 128 orthogonal directions (lesson 2). That, not the bit count, is the practical limit for one head.

blocks.prompt: Qwen3-Next's Gated DeltaNet layers have 36 x 32 = 1,152 heads of this size. Does that mean the model can recall about 1,152 x 8,192, roughly 9.4 million, facts from a prompt?
blocks.reveal: No. The bound is necessary, not sufficient: it says what *could* fit under an ideal code, while each head writes with one fixed learned rule, all heads in a layer see the same tokens, and reads are linear. Measured recall is far lower. In the Gated DeltaNet paper's S-NIAH-2 test, a single number hidden in 8K tokens of essays, the 1.3B Gated DeltaNet scores 29.6%.

blocks.md:
**State tracking.** The simplest case is **parity**: is the number of 1s seen so far odd? A two-state machine solves it by flipping on every 1. A linear RNN can do the same with one number, $h_t=a(x_t)h_{t-1}+b(x_t)$, using $a(1)=-1$, $b(1)=1$ and $a(0)=1$, $b(0)=0$ (Grazzi et al.). Each 1 maps h to 1 - h. The flip needs a **negative** transition.

In delta-rule form with a 1-dimensional key k = 1, a write is $S_t=(1-\beta_t)S_{t-1}+\beta_tv_t$. With $\beta=2$ and $v=0.5$ that is exactly $S_t=-S_{t-1}+1$ ($\beta=2$ is the edge of the extended range below; just under it, the flip is nearly exact). With $\beta\in(0,1)$ the factor $1-\beta$ is positive and the state can only creep toward $v$.

blocks.title: Parity of 1 1 0 1 1 1 with a 1-number state

scenes.caption: A 1 writes with strength beta and value v; a 0 sets beta = 0 (no change). The target is the parity row.
beta = 2, v = 0.5: S = -S + 1 on every 1. From 0 the state goes 1, 0, stays 0 on the 0 bit, then 1, 0, 1: exactly the parity.
beta = 0.6, v = 1: S = 0.4 S + 0.6. The state climbs 0.6, 0.84, 0.84, 0.936, 0.974, 0.990 toward 1 and never turns back, so no threshold separates odd from even for long inputs.

blocks.md: Grazzi et al. (ICLR 2025) prove the general version: a finite-precision linear RNN can solve parity at arbitrary lengths only if some transition has an eigenvalue that is not a nonnegative real number. Lesson 3's Householder matrix has eigenvalues 1 and $1-\beta_t$; with $\beta_t\in(0,1)$ and unit keys all lie in [0, 1], and Mamba2's $\alpha_t$ is in (0, 1) too. Their fix lets $\beta_t$ range over (0, 2), implemented as $I-2\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$, so $1-\beta$ reaches into (-1, 1). Trained on lengths 3 to 40 and tested on 40 to 256, parity scaled accuracy (1 is perfect, 0 is chance) went from 0.017 to 1.000 for DeltaNet and from 0.000 to 1.000 for Mamba; a Transformer scored 0.022. FLA's Gated DeltaNet layer exposes this as `allow_neg_eigval`, which scales $\beta$ to [0, 2).

Counting modulo 3 needs more: the same paper proves some product of transitions must have a complex eigenvalue, a rotation, which a diagonal or triangular real matrix cannot provide; products of Householder-like matrices can. DeltaProduct (Siems et al. 2025) takes $n_h$ delta steps per token, so each transition is a product of $n_h$ generalized Householder matrices (diagonal plus rank $n_h$), and reports better state tracking and language modeling than DeltaNet. RWKV-7 also admits eigenvalues outside [0, 1], though its pretrained models use only part of the negative range because of training instabilities.

Do not mix the two limits up. A bigger state helps recall but does nothing for parity: with eigenvalues in [0, 1], even a huge state fails at long lengths. Negative eigenvalues fix parity but add no storage. Production models answer the recall limit by keeping some attention layers (lesson 9).

blocks.question: A head has a $64\times64$ state stored in 16-bit numbers. What is the most random 32-bit values it could possibly store, under any encoding?
blocks.explain: 64 x 64 = 4,096 numbers, times 16 bits = 65,536 bits, divided by 32 bits per value = 2,048. Its linear read-out gives only about 64 clean slots, far fewer.

blocks.question: A DeltaNet with $\beta_t\in(0,1)$, unit keys and a state of one million numbers is trained on parity of short strings and tested on 1,000-bit strings. What do you expect?
options: It succeeds, because one million numbers can store 1,000 bits
It succeeds only if keys are not normalized
It succeeds once the gate $\alpha_t$ is added
It fails at long lengths: every transition's eigenvalues lie in [0, 1], whatever the state size
blocks.explain: Parity needs a flip, an eigenvalue that is negative (or complex). Storage is not the problem. Adding a gate in (0, 1) keeps eigenvalues nonnegative; extending beta to (0, 2) is the fix.

lessons.title: Decoding, serving and hybrid models in production

blocks.md:
Training uses the chunkwise kernel. Generation is different: tokens arrive one at a time, so each Gated DeltaNet layer runs the recurrent form once per token. Per sequence, a layer keeps two buffers and nothing else:

- the state, one $d_k\times d_v$ matrix per head (FLA's kernels and reference code default to [heads, d_k, d_v], the transpose of this course's $d_v\times d_k$; its GatedDeltaNet layer asks the kernels for the V-first layout [heads, d_v, d_k], this course's orientation);
- the short-convolution buffer: the last 4 inputs of each of the q, k and v convolutions (kernel width 4 in FLA and in Qwen3-Next's config).

For Qwen3-Next that is $32\times128\times128$ = 524,288 state numbers per layer plus 8,192 convolution channels times 4 positions = 32,768, about 6% extra.

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

H, dk, W = 4, 128, 4               # heads, head dim (d_k = d_v here), conv width
st = {"S": torch.zeros(H, dk, dk),             # state in FLA's kernel default [H, d_k, d_v]
      "conv": torch.zeros(3, H * dk, W)}       # last W inputs of the q, k, v convs

def decode_step(x, g, beta, conv_w, st):
    # x: [3, H*dk] projected q, k, v of ONE token; g, beta: [H] (alpha = exp(g))
    qkv = []
    for i in range(3):
        buf = torch.cat([st["conv"][i][:, 1:], x[i][:, None]], dim=1)  # drop oldest
        st["conv"][i] = buf
        qkv.append(F.silu((buf * conv_w[i]).sum(-1)).view(H, dk))     # causal conv
    q, k, v = qkv
    q, k = F.normalize(q, dim=-1) * dk ** -0.5, F.normalize(k, dim=-1)
    S = st["S"] * g.exp()[:, None, None]                    # gate the whole state
    v_old = torch.einsum("hk,hkv->hv", k, S)                # what memory returns for k
    S = S + beta[:, None, None] * torch.einsum("hk,hv->hkv", k, v - v_old)
    st["S"] = S
    return torch.einsum("hk,hkv->hv", q, S)                 # o = S q for every head

torch.manual_seed(0)
conv_w = torch.randn(3, H * dk, W)
for t in range(1000):                                       # generate 1,000 tokens
    o = decode_step(torch.randn(3, H * dk), -torch.rand(H), torch.rand(H), conv_w, st)
print(o.shape, st["S"].numel(), st["conv"].numel())        # memory never grew
blocks.caption: One decode step in FLA's kernel default layout, random inputs, CPU. Output: torch.Size([4, 128]) 65536 6144. After 1,000 tokens the state is still 4 x 128 x 128 numbers and the conv buffers 3 x 512 x 4. Without the conv, the same update matches FLA's naive_recurrent_gated_delta_rule to 1.2e-07.

blocks.md:
**Serving consequences.** The state is per sequence and fixed size: a 100-token chat and a 100K-token document hold the same state in every Gated DeltaNet layer, so memory per request is predictable. But nothing in it is per token. A KV cache can be cut into blocks of tokens and a shared prompt prefix reused block by block, which is how prefix caching works in engines such as vLLM; a recurrent state can only be reused as a whole snapshot taken exactly at the end of the shared prefix.

vLLM implements Gated DeltaNet as a Mamba-style layer ([source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/base.py)). With prefix caching on, its docs say the state is saved only at block boundaries, so a cache hit can resume only at a boundary; an optional flag adds a checkpoint where a shared prefix ends. The hybrid's attention layers keep their ordinary paged KV cache, and a request reuses the prefix that both kinds of layers have cached ([design doc](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/hybrid_kv_cache_manager.html)).

blocks.question: A hybrid model's serving engine snapshots Gated DeltaNet states every 512 tokens. A new request shares the first 1,000 tokens of its prompt with a cached request. From which position must it start computing?
options: Token 1, because recurrent states can never be shared
Token 993, after the last full 16-token KV block
Token 513, after the last saved state snapshot
Token 1,001, right after the shared prefix
blocks.explain: The attention layers could reuse almost all 1,000 tokens, but the Gated DeltaNet layers can only resume from a saved snapshot, the one after token 512. The engine takes the prefix both kinds of layers have, so tokens 513 to 1,000 are recomputed. A checkpoint at the end of the shared prefix would avoid that.

blocks.md: **Hybrids.** As lesson 8 showed, a fixed state cannot match attention at exact recall, so the paper also builds hybrids: **H1** interleaves Gated DeltaNet with sliding-window attention (window 2K: each token attends only to the 2K most recent tokens, so its KV cache stops growing), **H2** stacks Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window attention. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (80B parameters in total, about 3B activated per token) ships this idea: its config has 48 layers laid out as 12 repeats of (3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated full-attention, meaning ordinary softmax attention whose output is multiplied by a learned sigmoid gate), each followed by a mixture of experts layer: many feed-forward experts, of which a learned router picks a few for each token, which is why only about 3B of the 80B parameters are used per token. Kimi Linear similarly mixes KDA (Kimi Delta Attention), a Gated DeltaNet variant with finer-grained gating, with full multi-head latent attention layers (introduced in DeepSeek-V2, they cache one compressed latent vector per token instead of full keys and values).

How big is a KV cache? Per token and per layer it holds 2 (a key and a value) times the number of KV heads (grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key-value head, so this can be far smaller than the number of query heads) times the head dimension times the bytes per number. Qwen3-Next's attention layers let 16 query heads share 2 KV heads of dimension 256, stored as 16-bit numbers (2 bytes), so 2 x 2 x 256 x 2 = 2,048 bytes, which is 2 KiB. Here a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes and a mebibyte is 1,024 kibibytes.

blocks.title: Per-sequence cache in Qwen3-Next vs an all-attention variant

scenes.caption: From the config: attention layers have 2 KV heads of dim 256, so 2 x 2 x 256 x 2 bytes = 2 KiB per token per layer. An all-attention 48-layer variant (hypothetical) needs 96 KiB per token.

Hybrid = 12 attention layers (24 KiB per token) plus a fixed Gated DeltaNet state: 36 layers x 32 heads x 128 x 128 numbers = 72 MiB at 4 bytes. At 256K tokens: 6,216 vs 24,576 MiB. Simplified: ignores conv state.

blocks.md: The paper's 1.3B-parameter comparison has six models: Transformer++ (its softmax-attention baseline, a Transformer with the modern Llama-style recipe), Mamba2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet and the two hybrids H1 and H2, read in that order below. Commonsense accuracy is averaged over multiple-choice reasoning benchmarks, scored zero-shot. Real-world recall averages tasks whose answers must be found in a document given in the prompt.

blocks.title: 1.3B models on 100B tokens (paper Tables 3 and 4)

scenes.caption: Average zero-shot commonsense accuracy: 52.25, 54.89, 52.14, 55.32, 56.40, 56.18. Gated DeltaNet beats the other recurrent models; hybrids are best.
Average real-world recall (inputs truncated to 2K): 37.0, 29.8, 26.2, 30.6, 39.0, 40.1. Pure recurrent models still trail attention; adding attention layers closes the gap.

blocks.md: Do not read "linear" as "free". The paper measures Gated DeltaNet training throughput as essentially equal to DeltaNet but slightly below Mamba2, because its transition matrices are more expressive. And a pure linear model still loses to attention on recall-heavy tasks; production systems keep some attention layers. Choosing the ratio and placement of attention layers is a design question of its own; Qwen3-Next uses one attention layer in every four.

blocks.question: Qwen3-Next's context grows from 32K to 256K tokens. Which part of its per-sequence cache grows?
options: Only the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet state stays 72 MiB
Only the Gated DeltaNet state
Both grow 8x
Neither grows
blocks.explain: Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed $d_k\times d_v$ state per head regardless of length. The attention layers' KV cache grows linearly: 768 MiB at 32K to 6,144 MiB at 256K, while the 72 MiB state is unchanged.
